title: Thus it was said
hookLine: 112 short teachings, remembered by the laywoman Khujjuttara, a servant of the queen
carry: she came back with something better
last: FOR ONE WHO GIVES, MERIT GROWS.

cards: In the city of Kosambi, the story goes, Queen Samavati gives her servant money every day to buy flowers. And every day the servant, a woman named Khujjuttara, keeps some of the money for herself.
Then one day she hears the Buddha teach, and she comes home with the full amount, and all the flowers it buys. The queen notices. Khujjuttara confesses.
And then the queen asks her for something far more valuable than flowers.

teach.b: The queen and her women, the commentary says, couldn't leave the palace to hear the Buddha. So they asked Khujjuttara to go for them, and to bring the teaching home.

teach.h: SHE BROUGHT IT HOME, WORD FOR WORD.
teach.b: She went, she listened, and she came back and taught them, word for word, what she'd heard. The collection that tradition says grew from her memory is the Itivuttaka. Its name means thus it was said.

teach.h: THIS WAS SAID, SO I HEARD.
teach.b: Every one of its 112 short discourses opens with the same humble line: this was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I heard. Not I say. Not the Buddha says.
This was said, and I heard it: the voice of someone passing on what they were given, carefully, without adding. The teachings are arranged by number: a section of ones, of twos, of threes, of fours.
Each is short, a few lines of prose, then verse that says it again. Khujjuttara's name means the hunchbacked Uttara, and she was a servant.
Yet in the canon's list of outstanding disciples, she is named foremost among laywomen who had heard much.
In the tradition's telling, the person who kept these teachings wasn't a monk or a scholar or a queen. She was the woman sent to buy flowers.

how: The Itivuttaka is part of the Khuddaka Nikaya and is read and taught in Theravada communities; Khujjuttara is honored as a model of the learned lay disciple.

games.q: you're Khujjuttara. you've just heard the Buddha teach, and you've confessed to the queen about the flower money. the queen and her women can't leave the palace. what do they ask of you?
o: to go and hear the teaching and bring it home to them.
games.why: they ask her to be their ears. tradition says she taught them word for word, and the Itivuttaka is what she remembered.

practice: Think of one good thing someone taught you, a sentence, a habit, a way of seeing, that has stayed with you, and let the face of the person who said it come to mind.
Notice that you're a link in a chain, holding something that was handed to you, the way Khujjuttara carried the teachings home.

wordCard.voice: Itivuttaka. Thus it was said: 112 short teachings, each opening with this was said, so I heard, kept, tradition says, by the servant Khujjuttara. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali itivuttaka: 'thus it was said', from iti (thus) and vutta (said).

carryVoice: Your line: she came back with something better. Not only flowers, but the teaching, word for word. See you tomorrow.
